text.p: It was the nightmare on Wall Street.
The nation's central bank this week boosted interest rates for the first time in more than two years, reinforcing its inflation-fighting credentials.
At the same time, the Federal Reserve's move reminded stock investors that bull markets don't die of old age but instead, they are slaughtered by interest rate hikes.
The Fed's quarter-point increase in the key federal funds rate to 5.50 percent, which was widely expected, triggered a sell-off in stocks.

By the end of an abbreviated trading week, the Dow Jones industrial average Thursday closed with a huge loss of 140.11 points at 6,740.59, which was sharply off its record closing high of 7,085.16 set on March 11. For the week, it was down 64.20 points. Financial markets were shut for Good Friday.
Commercial banks didn't waste any time reacting, boosting their prime lending rates, which are linked to credit cards, adjustable mortgages and home equity loans, to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent.

But Wall Streets was clearly worried that the Fed's pre-emptive action was not over, and they geared for more interest rates hikes in the months ahead, which could stop the longest bull market run in its tracks.
The stock market hates higher rates because they tend to slow the economy and eat into corporate profits.

"I'm beginning to think that maybe the cockroach theory is coming true, that when you see one interest rate increase, there will be more increases," said James Dines, publisher of the Dines Letter, in Belvedere, Calif.

Investors recalled vividly that in 1994, the Fed started to raise interest rates to prevent the economy from overheating. When word got out that interest rates were headed higher, stocks plunged 10 percent and finished 1994 on a flat note.

The market went nowhere until Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan stopped raising rates in February 1995, but only after seven increases that doubled the fed funds rate, which banks charge each other for overnight loans, from 3 percent to 6 percent and brought the economy to the brink of recession.
The good times returned to Wall Street later in 1995, as stocks jumped 33.5 percent and climbed 26 percent in 1996.

The central bankers' theme this week was that an increase was needed as a "prudent step" to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year. And, it hinted at more action to come.

Critics say price pressures in the economy are still holding at the lowest levels in decades, and they believe that the Fed is actually gunning for the overly bullish stock market investors in the guise of fighting inflation demons.

After more than six years of expansion, inflation remains in check. Consumer prices were up just 0.3 percent in February after edging up 0.1 percent in January, providing more proof that intense global competition is offering protection against the threat of serious inflation.
For the last two years, inflation has been tame. Consumer prices inched up only 3.3 percent in 1996 after a 2.5 percent rise in 1995.

The stock market has been hitting record highs for more than two years on steady earnings growth and low inflation, ignoring warnings from Greenspan that investors may have thrown caution to the wind in boosting stock prices by some 60 percent since 1995.

"Greenspan is trying to draw fire away from one demon by creating another demon, and in this case it's the great volatility of the stock market that he is worried about," said John Geraghty at the consulting firm, North American Equity Services.

"By talking up inflation, he's talking away from more serious problems, which he can't control, and it's the billions of dollars that are going into mutual funds and are driving financial markets," he said.
For the first time, the buying frenzy that has propelled stocks to dizzying heights is causing concern among central bankers, who realise that a market meltdown could stun the economy.

Ageing Baby Boomers have been socking away money for their retirement years and the mutual funds assets as of February stood at $3.7 trillion, up from $3.5 trillion in December, according to the Investment Company Institute, a Washington-based mutual fund trade group. In 1995, mutual fund asssets totalled $2.8 trillion.

Greg Smith, chief investment stategist at Prudential Securities says the Fed may have a very good reason to worry about the stock market, now that the mutual fund assets' of $3.7 trillion and are fast approaching the $4.5 trillion in total assets for U.S. commercial banks.
Last year, the banks' assets grew by less than 6 percent vs. an eye-popping 26 percent gain for mutual funds.
"Not only are mutual fund assets rivaling the economic power of the banking system, but the equity market last year was the source of $115 billion of new capital," he said.

"This compares with about a $150 billion increase in commercial banking total loans and leases," Smith said. "Including capital raised in the bond markets, financial markets clearly surpass commercial banks as sources of capital."
He said that the Fed was now in the position of having to "control" financial markets in order to contain the nation's economic activity.

The Nasdaq composite index fell 19.57 points Thursday to 1,249.51, for a loss of 4.56 on the week. The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks sank 16.62 points to 773.88 and lost 10.22 for the week.
The American Stock Exchange index fell 5.17 to 577.90 and was off 13.32 on the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 7.94 to 407.43, which was down 5.37 on the week.
